questions.title: A and B together can complete a project in 12 days...
questions.question: A and B together can complete a project in 12 days. B and C together can complete it in 15 days, while C and A together can do it in 20 days. How many days will A alone take to finish the work?
questions.explanation:
Work rate equation: 2(A + B + C) = 1/12 + 1/15 + 1/20 = (5 + 4 + 3)/60 = 12/60 = 1/5.
So A + B + C = 1/10 per day.
A's 1-day work = (A + B + C) - (B + C) = 1/10 - 1/15 = (3 - 2)/30 = 1/30.
Therefore, A alone takes 30 days.

questions.title: Calculating Selling Price with consecutive discounts
questions.question: An item priced at ₹2,000 is sold with two successive discounts of 20% and 10%. What is the final selling price?

questions.title: Find the missing number in the matrix pattern
questions.question: In a given sequence: 4, 18, 48, 100, 180, ? . What is the next number?
questions.explanation:
Pattern formula: n² × (n + 1) or n³ - n².
1st term (n=1): 1² × (1+1) = 2 (Skip/Base)
2nd term (n=2): 2² × 1 = 4
3rd term (n=3): 3² × 2 = 18
4th term (n=4): 4² × 3 = 48
5th term (n=5): 5² × 4 = 100
6th term (n=6): 6² × 5 = 180
7th term (n=7): 7² × 6 = 49 × 6 = 294.

questions.title: Two Sum - Target Pair in an Array
questions.question: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target. What is the optimal time complexity achievable using a Hash Map?
questions.explanation: By storing elements in a HashMap as key-value pairs (element -> index), we can check if `target - nums[i]` exists in the HashMap in O(1) average time. Traversing the array once yields O(N) time complexity and O(N) auxiliary space.

questions.title: Difference between WHERE and HAVING clause
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes between the `WHERE` and `HAVING` clauses in SQL?
options: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups created by GROUP BY.
HAVING can be used without GROUP BY, but WHERE cannot.
WHERE is used only with aggregate functions like SUM() and COUNT().
There is no functional difference; they are interchangeable.
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual record rows before aggregation occurs. HAVING is specifically used to filter summarized aggregate results after GROUP BY is applied.

questions.title: Deadlock Conditions (Coffman Conditions)
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four necessary Coffman conditions for a system deadlock to occur?
questions.explanation: The four Coffman conditions are: 1. Mutual Exclusion, 2. Hold and Wait, 3. No Preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken), 4. Circular Wait. 'Preemption Allowed' prevents deadlock rather than causing it.

questions.title: Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) in Binary Search Tree
questions.question: In a Binary Search Tree (BST), if nodes p and q both have values smaller than the root value, where does their Lowest Common Ancestor lie?
options: In the right subtree of the root
In the left subtree of the root
It is the root node itself
questions.explanation: By BST properties, all values in the left subtree are smaller than the root. If both node values p and q are less than root.val, LCA must exist inside the left subtree.

questions.title: 0/1 Knapsack Problem Complexity
questions.question: What is the time complexity of the classic 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming solution with N items and maximum capacity W?
questions.explanation: The 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming table has (N+1) rows and (W+1) columns. Filling each cell takes O(1) time, resulting in O(N × W) pseudo-polynomial time complexity.

questions.title: TCP vs UDP Protocol Differences
questions.question: Which network protocol is connection-oriented, guarantees ordered packet delivery, and provides error checking via acknowledgment?
questions.explanation: TCP performs a 3-way handshake to establish a reliable, connection-oriented session with flow control and error recovery. UDP is connectionless and unacknowledged.

hrGuide.question: Tell me about yourself.
hrGuide.tip: Keep it under 90 seconds. Structure: Past (Education/Background) -> Present (Current skills & projects) -> Future (Why this company fits your ambition).
hrGuide.sampleAnswer: I am a final-year Computer Science student passionate about full-stack engineering and problem solving. During my academics, I built web applications using JavaScript and Python, including a real-time collaborative tool. Recently, I solved 250+ DSA problems on LeetCode focusing on efficient algorithms. I'm excited about this opportunity because your engineering team scales solutions for millions of users.

hrGuide.question: What is your biggest weakness and how do you work on it?
hrGuide.tip: Pick a real professional skill you are actively improving. Never say 'I am a perfectionist' or 'I work too hard'.
hrGuide.sampleAnswer: Earlier, I used to get absorbed in trying to solve complex debugging issues alone for hours before reaching out. I realized this could impact team timelines. Now, I follow a strict 30-minute rule: if I'm stuck after thoroughly researching for 30 minutes, I summarize my hypothesis and consult a team member.

hrGuide.question: Describe a difficult situation you faced during a project and how you handled it.
hrGuide.tip: Use the STAR Method: Situation -> Task -> Action -> Result.
hrGuide.sampleAnswer: Situation: Two days before our final semester demo, our database queries started timing out under load. Task: I needed to optimize query latency without re-architecting the database schema. Action: I analyzed query execution plans, indexed high-cardinality foreign keys, and implemented client-side caching. Result: Latency dropped by 75% and our demo received an A grade.
